whoIsThisFor.heading: Who should take the Marketing Cloud Engagement Foundations exam?

personas.label: New Marketing Cloud Engagement users
personas.description: You have started using Engagement and want a credential showing that you can navigate its basic features.

personas.label: Marketers changing platforms
personas.description: You know campaign and email concepts from another tool and want to learn Salesforce’s Marketing Cloud terms.

personas.label: Admins taking on Marketing Cloud
personas.description: You have become responsible for a Marketing Cloud account and need to build a working foundation.

examDifficulty.heading: How challenging is the Marketing Cloud Engagement Foundations exam?
examDifficulty.summary: This introductory exam is aimed at people with up to six months of Marketing Cloud Engagement experience. It checks basic navigation, email sending, the difference between lists and data extensions, and tracking reports. It does not require coding or data architecture skills.
bullets: 40 scored questions in 70 minutes, plus up to five unscored questions that do not count.
65% to pass, which is 26 correct answers out of 40.
Broad platform knowledge. Know the purpose of each studio rather than advanced configuration.
Exam fee: US$75. Check current pricing before booking.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Practise in a Marketing Cloud org: create a data extension, build an email in Content Builder, send it to an audience, and find its opens and clicks. Repeat any step that still feels unfamiliar.

examFormat.heading: Marketing Cloud Engagement Foundations exam format
examFormat.intro: The exam is proctored online or at a test centre. Questions cover platform basics and common tasks.
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Some questions describe a sending or reporting situation. You may need to select an audience source or interpret an email tracking result.
bestWayToPass: Work in the platform: Hands-on use helps you learn the interface and the purpose of each tool.
Compare lists and data extensions: Lists are the older subscriber model; data extensions are customizable tables used for many modern audiences.
Send a test email: Build content, select an audience and send classification, test the message, then review tracking.
Know bounce behavior: Distinguish temporary soft bounces from permanent hard bounces and understand their effect on subscribers.

certificationCard.description: This introductory credential covers core Marketing Cloud Engagement tasks, including content creation, subscriber and data-extension audiences, automation, journeys, and send tracking. The exam is 40 scored questions in 70 minutes, with a 65% pass mark, weighted towards Marketing Concepts (28%) and Marketing Cloud Engagement Basics (22%).

keyConcepts.h2: Marketing Cloud Engagement Foundations: concepts to know

blocks.heading: Email Studio and Content Builder
blocks.body: Content Builder stores emails, images, and reusable content blocks. Build an email from a template, place blocks in its regions, and personalize it with AMPscript or personalization strings that read from the send audience. Shared blocks update wherever they are used, which saves effort but can affect several emails at once. A send requires three parts: the email, an audience, and a send classification containing sender and delivery profiles. If a send cannot start, check that all three are configured.

blocks.heading: Lists, data extensions, and Contact Builder
blocks.body: Subscriber lists are the older audience model. They use a subscriber key and a set of account-level profile and preference attributes. A data extension is a table whose columns and primary key you define, so it works for custom fields and larger data models. Contact Builder connects contact data across channels by contact key and lets you define relationships between data. A basic newsletter may use a list; use a data extension when you need custom fields or more control.

blocks.heading: Automation Studio
blocks.body: Automation Studio runs sequences on a schedule or when a file arrives in an FTP folder. Common activities include imports, SQL queries that write to a data extension, file transfers, extracts, and sends. A typical workflow imports a file, queries it to build a segment, and sends an email. Automation Studio handles scheduled or batch work; Journey Builder manages an individual contact’s path over time. An Automation Studio SQL Query activity writes to a configured target data extension.

blocks.heading: Journey Builder
blocks.body: A journey moves individual contacts from an entry source, such as a data extension or API event, through sends, waits, decisions, and updates. Entry settings determine how often the source is checked and whether a contact can enter again. A decision split uses stored contact data; an engagement split responds to an open or click. Journeys are versioned. To change one that is running, create and activate a new version.

blocks.heading: Tracking and reporting
blocks.body: Tracking reports show sends, deliveries, opens, clicks, and bounces. Delivered is sent minus bounces; engagement rates use delivered messages as their base. A hard bounce indicates a permanent address failure, so the subscriber becomes undeliverable. A soft bounce is temporary, such as a full mailbox, and the platform retries. Unsubscribes normally update the All Subscribers status unless publication lists are used. Email Studio provides job-level tracking; Analytics Builder offers broader reporting.

scenarioTips.h2: How to prepare for the Marketing Cloud Engagement Foundations exam
scenarioTips.intro: The exam checks basic platform use. Practise common tasks in Marketing Cloud rather than relying only on notes.

blocks.heading: Know each studio
blocks.body: Learn the purpose of Email Studio, Mobile Studio, Advertising Studio, Journey Builder, Automation Studio, Content Builder, Contact Builder, and Analytics Builder.

blocks.heading: Choose between lists and data extensions
blocks.body: Understand subscriber keys, list attributes, and why data extensions suit custom fields and structured data.

blocks.heading: Complete a guided send
blocks.body: Build an email, select the audience and send classification, send a test, then review tracking.

blocks.heading: Understand bounces and unsubscribes
blocks.body: Compare hard and soft bounces, know how subscriber status changes, and know where unsubscribes are recorded.

blocks.heading: Read send reports
blocks.body: Know how delivered, open, click, and bounce metrics are calculated and what the numbers show.

sampleQuestions.question: A marketer needs 20 customer-specific fields, including purchase history and loyalty tier, for personalization. What audience storage fits?
options: A suppression list
A data extension with the required columns
A publication list
A subscriber list with shared profile attributes
sampleQuestions.explanation: Data extensions let the marketer define the fields needed for each customer record.
whyWrong: Suppression lists identify addresses to exclude from sends.
Publication lists manage subscriber opt-outs rather than custom customer fields.
List profile attributes are account-level and not suited to this many record-specific fields.

sampleQuestions.question: The email and audience exist, but a send cannot be launched. Which required item is most likely missing?
options: A second data extension
A new journey version
An Analytics Builder report
A send classification
sampleQuestions.explanation: A send needs an email, an audience, and a send classification with sender and delivery profiles.
whyWrong: The send does not need a second audience by default.
Journeys are separate from an Email Studio send.
Reports are created after a send and do not enable it.

sampleQuestions.question: What happens after a subscriber’s email address hard bounces?
options: The subscriber joins a publication list
The address is marked permanently undeliverable
The system retries for several days
The address is treated as a temporary failure
sampleQuestions.explanation: A hard bounce signals a permanent address problem, so the platform stops sending to that address.
whyWrong: Publication lists control communication preferences.
Retries are associated with temporary soft bounces.
Temporary failure describes a soft bounce, not a hard bounce.

sampleQuestions.question: A nightly workflow must import an FTP file, create a segment with SQL, and send an email. Which tool should run this process?
options: Journey Builder
Changes wait until each email is republished separately
Automation Studio
Content Builder
sampleQuestions.explanation: Automation Studio runs scheduled or file-triggered sequences such as imports, queries, and sends.
whyWrong: Journey Builder handles contact-level journeys rather than scheduled batch sequences.
Contact Builder manages contact data and relationships.
Content Builder stores email content and assets.

sampleQuestions.question: In Journey Builder, how does a decision split differ from an engagement split?
options: They are two names for the same feature
A decision split runs faster
Stored attributes versus engagement activity
An engagement split can appear only once in a journey
sampleQuestions.explanation: Decision splits evaluate existing attributes. Engagement splits respond to behavior such as an email open or click.
whyWrong: The two split types evaluate different information.
Execution speed is not the distinction.
There is no single-use rule for engagement splits.

sampleQuestions.question: A marketer wants new journey entrants to receive an updated email while contacts already in the active journey continue unchanged. What should they do?
options: Create and activate a new journey version
Pause Automation Studio
Edit the running version directly
Delete the journey and rebuild it
sampleQuestions.explanation: Publish a new journey version with the revised email. Contacts already in the active version can continue there, while new entrants use the newly activated version.
whyWrong: Automation Studio is not required to update a journey.
A running version cannot be edited in place.
Versioning avoids deleting journey history.

sampleQuestions.question: A subscriber unsubscribes from an email. What is the default account-level result?
options: Remove the subscriber record entirely
Delete the data extension row
Set the All Subscribers status to unsubscribed
Block only the message they clicked
sampleQuestions.explanation: Unless publication lists are used, the unsubscribe is recorded at All Subscribers level.
whyWrong: The record remains, with its status changed.
Unsubscribing does not delete stored data.
A one-message opt-out is not the default behavior.

sampleQuestions.question: A shared Content Builder block is edited. What happens to emails that reference it?
options: Each email receives a separate copy
Changes wait until each email is republished
Only emails created later use the new block
The change applies wherever the block is used
sampleQuestions.explanation: Reusable blocks are shared, so editing one updates the content for every email that uses it.
whyWrong: Referenced content is not duplicated for each email.
No separate republish step is needed for shared content.
Existing emails also use the shared block.

sampleQuestions.question: How is the delivered count in an email tracking report calculated?
options: Sent minus bounces
Sent minus unsubscribes
Audience size before exclusions
Opens plus clicks
sampleQuestions.explanation: Delivered is the number sent minus messages that bounced.
whyWrong: Unsubscribes are tracked separately.
The audience may be larger than the final sent count.
Opens and clicks are engagement actions, not deliveries.

sampleQuestions.question: Which identifier connects a contact’s records across Marketing Cloud channels?
options: The journey version
A record ID
The email address
The contact key
sampleQuestions.explanation: The contact key is the identifier used to connect a person’s records across channels.
whyWrong: A journey version identifies a journey release, not a contact.
Core Salesforce record IDs do not serve as the Marketing Cloud cross-channel key.
Email addresses can change and are not the cross-channel identifier.

sampleQuestions.question: Subscribers should be able to opt out of a newsletter but continue to receive transactional mail. What should the marketer use?
options: A publication list for the newsletter
A second contact key per subscriber
A separate Marketing Cloud account
A suppression list containing every subscriber
sampleQuestions.explanation: Publication lists let subscribers opt out of a category while remaining eligible for other communications.
whyWrong: Multiple keys fragment a contact’s history.
A separate account is unnecessary for category-level preferences.
Suppressing everyone blocks all mail.

sampleQuestions.question: Where does a SQL Query activity in Automation Studio write its results?
options: By emailing them to the account owner
By displaying them in an on-screen grid
To its configured target data extension
To a new subscriber list automatically
sampleQuestions.explanation: The query activity writes results to the target data extension selected in its configuration.
whyWrong: Query results are not emailed automatically.
The scheduled query does not open an interactive results grid.
The target is a data extension, not a subscriber list.

sampleQuestions.question: When should a journey check its entry source more frequently?
options: When the account has multiple business units
New contacts should enter during the day
When the journey contains several decision splits
When email open rates are low
sampleQuestions.explanation: Entry evaluation frequency determines how quickly new eligible contacts are added.
whyWrong: Business unit structure does not determine entry frequency.
The number of splits does not affect the entry check.
Open rates relate to message performance, not entry timing.

sampleQuestions.question: Why send a test email before a campaign send?
options: To check rendering and personalization
To generate the final tracking report
To count the audience
To warm up a dedicated IP address
sampleQuestions.explanation: A test lets the marketer review how content and personalization appear before sending to the full audience.
whyWrong: Tracking reports are produced from the campaign send.
Audience counts are available during send setup.
IP warming is a separate deliverability activity.

sampleQuestions.question: Which statement about soft bounces is correct?
options: They indicate a permanent address failure
Temporary failures can be retried
They count as delivered messages
They automatically unsubscribe the contact
sampleQuestions.explanation: A soft bounce is a temporary delivery problem, such as a full mailbox, so the platform can retry.
whyWrong: Permanent failure describes a hard bounce.
A bounced message was not delivered.
Bounces and unsubscribes are separate statuses.
